opus-5.5.text:
That's a really important question, and honestly it's one of the things we thought about a lot when designing our "Mission: Impossible Language Models" experiments. The way we constructed impossible languages was by taking a natural language corpus, in our case English data from the BabyLM dataset, and applying systematic perturbations to it. We shuffled word order, reversed sentences, or introduced counting-based grammar rules that no human language would use. So every impossible language we studied was defined relative to that English starting point.

That design has real advantages. You control for vocabulary, content, and a lot of distributional properties, so when you see a difference in how easily a model learns the natural version versus the perturbed version, you can attribute it more confidently to the structural manipulation itself. But it also means your conclusions are tied to the properties of English. English has fairly rigid word order and relatively little morphology, so a word-order perturbation might be much more disruptive for English than it would be for a language with freer word order and rich case marking, where the information is carried in the morphology.

So I think future work should really broaden the set of starting corpora. Ideally you'd take typologically diverse languages, say a head-final language like Japanese, a morphologically rich language like Turkish or Finnish, maybe a free word order language, and apply comparable perturbations to each. Then you can ask whether the gap between possible and impossible holds consistently, or whether some of what we called "impossible" is really just "unlike English." You'd also want to think carefully about what counts as a comparable perturbation across languages, because a deterministic shuffle or a reversal interacts differently with each language's structure.

There's also a tokenization angle. Tokenizers are usually trained on the natural corpus, and that can quietly give the natural language an advantage, or interact strangely with the perturbations. So being explicit about how the tokenizer was built, and ideally controlling for that, matters as well.

More broadly, I'd encourage people to be transparent that the starting corpus is a real experimental variable, not just a convenience. The claims we want to make about language models and human-like inductive biases are ultimately about the space of human languages, not about English. Getting there means sampling that space more carefully.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using typologically diverse source languages and applying comparable perturbations to each, allowing comparison of each natural language with its derived impossible version.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the starting corpus is doing more work than people usually acknowledge, and we should be upfront about that rather than treating it as a neutral detail.

In our work, we started from a natural language dataset, English text, essentially the kind of data a language model would normally be trained on, and then we applied systematic perturbations to it to create the impossible counterparts. Things like reversing word order, shuffling tokens either fully or in local windows, or inserting markers that force the model to count tokens for things like verb agreement. The appeal of that design is control. Every impossible language is derived from exactly the same underlying sentences, so the information content and the vocabulary are matched, and the only thing that differs is the structural manipulation. If you see a gap in how well models learn them, you can attribute it to that structural difference rather than to the corpus being bigger or messier or about different topics.

But there's a catch, and it's one I think the field should take seriously. The natural language baseline is, by construction, the most natural thing in the comparison. All of the impossible variants are deformations of it. So you have to ask whether your results are telling you something about learnability in general, or something about distance from this particular corpus. We tried to address that partially by including a control that was already essentially random, so we had a kind of floor, and by varying how severe the perturbations were, so we could see a gradient rather than a binary. That gradient was actually one of the more convincing pieces of evidence for us, because it showed the models tracked something like how impossible the language was, not just whether it matched English.

Going forward, I'd want to see a few things. First, don't rely on English alone. If you run the same perturbations starting from a typologically different language, say one with freer word order or richer morphology, and the pattern holds, that's much stronger. Second, think about the size and domain of the corpus. The claims being tested here come out of linguistics, and they're about what humans acquire from the input children actually get. A web-scale corpus is a very different thing from child-directed speech, and the conclusions you can draw shift depending on which one you pick. And third, be explicit about what the baseline is supposed to represent. If you're comparing to "natural language," you should say which natural language, in which register, and why that stands in for the category.

So I don't think there's a single right corpus. I think the right move is to treat the corpus choice as part of the experimental design, state the assumptions clearly, and then test whether the findings survive when you change it.

r001.rationale: The response proposes applying the same perturbations to a typologically different source language and comparing the resulting pattern, extending comparisons of natural languages with their derived impossible variants across multiple sources.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting corpus is something you want to treat as an experimental variable, because it brings a lot of structure into the comparison. If you start with English and transform it to create an impossible language, you're still inheriting properties of English, even if you've changed the word order. So that experiment can tell you something useful, but it doesn't necessarily tell you how natural and impossible languages compare more generally.

Ideally, you'd repeat the experiment with starting corpora from several typologically different languages, while keeping things like the amount of data and the domain as comparable as possible. Then you can ask whether the result holds across those starting points or whether it depends on a particular property of the original corpus. The important thing is to distinguish an effect of the transformation from an effect of the language you started with.

r001.rationale: The response recommends repeating the transformation experiment with starting corpora from several typologically different languages, comparing each starting point with its transformed impossible language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting corpus is something we should treat as an experimental variable, rather than just a neutral input. If we take an English corpus and transform it to create an impossible language, that gives us a useful controlled comparison, but the result is still tied to English—its vocabulary, its distribution of constructions, and the particular texts we chose.

So I’d want to repeat those experiments starting from different natural languages, ideally ones with quite different grammatical properties, and also across different kinds of text. Within each comparison, we should keep things like the amount of training data and the content as comparable as possible. That would help us distinguish a preference for natural-language structure from a preference that happens to depend on the starting corpus.

r001.rationale: The response proposes repeating the comparison from different natural-language starting corpora, referring back to experiments that transform each corpus to create an impossible language.
